pamphlet_excerpts: Constitutional Protection: The First Amendment shields independent reporting from government prior restraint and political censorship.
Defamation Standards: Published false written statements that harm personal reputation constitute legally actionable civil libel.
Slander Liability: Spoken false statements damaging professional reputation create grounds for immediate civil slander lawsuits.
Fair Comment Defense: Editorial opinions regarding matters of public interest receive protection under common law doctrines.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Source Verification: Cross check controversial claims across two independent documentary records before publication.
Step 2 - Statement Classification: Mark subjective value judgements separately from objectively verifiable statements in your draft.
Step 3 - Defamation Review: Scan manuscript copy to eliminate unverified claims damaging individual character or business standing.
Step 4 - Legal Consultation: Submit disputed investigative findings to legal counsel to confirm fair comment protections.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Journalism Requirement 1, why does the First Amendment protect freedom of the press in a democracy, and how must a responsible journalist distinguish straight news reporting from an editorial or opinion column?
quiz_item.question: In Journalism Requirement 1, why does the First Amendment protect freedom of the press in a democracy, and how must a responsible journalist distinguish straight news reporting from an editorial or opinion column?
options: A. Freedom of the press allows reporters to publish fabricated quotes and defamatory falsehoods without checking any sources.
B. A straight news article should express the reporter's personal political endorsements in the opening paragraph and omit opposing.
C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable.
D. Journalists are required by federal law to submit every local newspaper article to city hall for censorship before printing.
choices: A. Freedom of the press allows reporters to publish fabricated quotes and defamatory falsehoods without checking any sources.
B. A straight news article should express the reporter's personal political endorsements in the opening paragraph and omit opposing.
C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable.
D. Journalists are required by federal law to submit every local newspaper article to city hall for censorship before printing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. An independent press informs citizens and holds government and institutions accountable.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A free press enables informed self-governance, and journalistic ethics require rigorous multi-source fact verification, fairness, and a clear separation between objective news reporting and labeled opinion/editorial writing.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Option A, Newspaper, Magazine, and Online Journalism. (Ask your parent or guardian's permission for the online option.) Do ALL of the following: (1) On the same day, read a local news source or newspaper, a national news source or newspaper, a news magazine (online or printed), and a social media news feed. From each source, clip, read, and compare a story about the same event. Tell your counselor how long each story is and how fair and accurate the stories are in presenting different points of view. Tell how each source handled the story. (2) Visit the office of a newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Ask for a tour of the various divisions (editorial, business, and printing). During your tour, talk to an executive from the business side about management's relations with reporters, editors, and photographers, and what makes a "good" newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Note: If there are no opportunities for in-person visits in your community, a virtual visit is acceptable with the news site of your choice, provided your counselor approves this option in advance. (You can request a virtual visit with Scout Life magazine ) (b) Option B, Radio and Television Journalism. Do ALL of the following: (1) All on the same day, watch a local and national network newscast, listen to a radio newscast, and (with your parent or guardian's permission) view a national broadcast news source online. List the different news items and features presented, the different elements used, and the time in minutes and seconds and the online space devoted to each story. Compare the story lists and discuss whether the stories are fair and accurate. Explain why different news outlets treated the stories differently and/or presented a different point of view. (2) Visit a radio or television station. Ask for a tour of the various departments, concentrating on those related to news broadcasts. During your tour, talk to the station manager or other station management executive about station operations, particularly how management and the news staff work together, and what makes a "good" station. If possible, go with a reporter to cover a news event.
